concepts.title: The Father's Order and the Felling
concepts.definition: Dilip Chitre's autobiographical poem begins with an order: the father tells the tenants to leave the houses around their hillside home, and the trees are cut one by one. The great banyan, oldest and largest, three times taller than a man, with aerial roots and thirty-foot trunk, is finally butchered with saws and axes.
concepts.key_idea: Progress with an axe -- a father's order erases a landscape and a hundred years of shade.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww120.txt opening sections (father told tenants to leave, houses demolished, banyan tree oldest and largest, aerial roots, saws and axes)

solution_steps.explain: The father's modernising decision clears tenants, houses and then the trees around the hill house.
The banyan -- grandest of all, with hanging roots and massive trunk -- embodies rootedness in age and size.
Saws work through the trunk in segments; the felling is described with clinical, shocking detail.

concepts.title: Massacre Reported as News: The Son's Alienated Gaze
concepts.definition: The boy watches the felling from a safe distance, and the poem calls it a massacre -- yet he admits he took no part and felt no personal connection to the tree. This split voice -- sorrow and detachment together -- makes the son a witness rather than a mourner, reporting his father's world as alien.
concepts.key_idea: A massacre watched from the window -- the son grieves a tree he never knew, and feels the estrangement more.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww120.txt middle sections (watching from a distance, massacre imagery, the poet took no part, no personal attachment admitted, father as figure of modernity)

solution_steps.explain: Words like massacre frame tree-felling as killing -- the boy's private verdict on his father's project.
He owns that he had no real bond with the tree, watching the destruction like news from elsewhere.
The deeper theme is displacement: modernity has alienated the son from both root and rite.

concepts.title: Farewell to the Banyan: Exile and Rootedness
concepts.definition: The poem closes with a farewell: soon afterwards the family moves to Bombay, where no trees could grow. The banyan becomes the poet's last memory of rooted country life -- a shrine remembered in dreams -- so that the felled tree turns into an emblem of uprooting, of a childhood and a landscape lost to change.
concepts.key_idea: The tree felled, the family exiled -- memory of the banyan becomes the poet's only rooted ground.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww120.txt closing sections (move to bombay, no trees in the city, farewell to the tree, memory and dreams of the banyan, theme of uprooting)

solution_steps.explain: They shift to Bombay where apartments leave no room for banyans -- exile completed.
In memory the banyan grows back: root, trunk and shade become shorthand for all that was left behind.
Chitre's poem mourns ecological loss and human uprooting in the same breath -- each felling a small exile.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Why does the poet choose the word 'massacre' instead of a neutral word like 'cutting'?

solution_template.explain: Massacre implies the killing of beings, not the trimming of plants.
To the watching child the axe-work on a century-old giant feels exactly like slaughter.
The word carries the poem's judgment on progress that kills what it cannot value.

worked_examples.question_pattern: How does the move to Bombay complete the meaning of the felling in the poem?

solution_template.explain: The tree is felled to build; the family then moves to a city of buildings where trees cannot grow.
What is lost is both a landscape and a way of being rooted in one.
The banyan's felling foreshadows the family's own uprooting -- poem and life share one theme.
